passages.happening:
After the defeat at Kadesh, Israel turned back into the wilderness, ‘and for many days we wandered around Mount Seir’ (verse 1). Then God said, “You have been wandering around this hill country long enough; turn to the north” (verse 3).

The road north ran past Edom, the people descended from Esau. God gave strict orders. “Do not provoke them, for I will not give you any of their land, not even a footprint, because I have given Mount Seir to Esau as his possession” (verse 5). Israel was to pay in silver for its food and water (verse 6).

Moses adds a word about the years just ended: “The LORD your God has been with you these forty years, and you have lacked nothing” (verse 7). So Israel passed by Edom and took the road toward Moab (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Esau was the twin brother of Jacob, the father of Israel. That is why God calls the Edomites ‘your brothers’. Their land, Mount Seir, lay south of the Dead Sea.

The surprise of this passage is whose side God takes. Israel is the chosen people, on its way to a promised land. A hearer might expect every land on the road to be theirs for the taking. God says no. He has given Seir to Esau. Israel may not have a footprint of it.

The word translated ‘possession’ is the same word used for Israel's own land. God has assigned this hill country to Edom in the way he will assign Canaan to Israel. He is the God of more nations than one.

There is a touch of irony in verse 4. ‘They will be afraid of you, so you must be very careful.’ A generation earlier Israel had been the frightened one. Now it is told not to take advantage of someone else's fear.

To pass through another people's land, a traveling people would ask leave and pay for what it ate and drank. Israel is told to deal honestly, as a guest and not as a raider.

Verse 7 is Moses' summary of forty years that were also a punishment. The wilderness was where a generation died. It was also where God never left. Moses holds both together: the years were hard, and nothing needed was missing.
passages.later:
Genesis tells where Edom came from: “So Esau (that is, Edom) settled in the area of Mount Seir” (Genesis 36:8).

Later in this book the tie is made a law: “Do not despise an Edomite, for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7).

Nehemiah, praying centuries later, repeated Moses' summary of the wilderness: “For forty years You sustained them in the wilderness, so that they lacked nothing” (Nehemiah 9:21).

Paul told the philosophers of Athens that God made every nation, ‘and He determined their appointed times and the boundaries of their lands’ (Acts 17:26).
passages.asks: God told his own people that another people's land was not theirs to take. Ask whether you assume that being loved by God means others must give way to you. And look back over your own hardest years with verse 7 in hand. Ask what was given in them that you needed.

passages.t: Moab, Ammon, and the end of a generation
passages.happening:
The same order comes for Moab. “Do not harass the Moabites or provoke them to war, for I will not give you any of their land, because I have given Ar to the descendants of Lot as their possession” (verse 9).

Israel crosses the Brook of Zered. Moses counts the time: from Kadesh to this crossing ‘was thirty-eight years, until that entire generation of fighting men had perished from the camp, as the LORD had sworn to them’ (verse 14).

Then the order comes a third time, for Ammon. “I have given it to the descendants of Lot as their possession” (verse 19).

Twice the speech stops for a note about the peoples who lived in these lands long before: the Emites in Moab, the Horites in Seir, the Zamzummites in Ammon, and the Avvim near Gaza (verses 10-12 and 20-23).
passages.hearers:
Moab and Ammon were descended from Lot, the nephew of Abraham. Moab lay east of the Dead Sea, and Ammon further north and east. Like Edom, they were Israel's relatives, and their lands were not on offer.

Three times in this chapter God says of another people, ‘I have given’. The repetition makes the point. Israel's God had been at work among other nations before Israel arrived, settling them in their places.

The notes in brackets read like a historian's aside. They record old traditions about earlier peoples, remembered as tall and many. The Emites and Zamzummites were counted among the Rephaim. The Caphtorites of verse 23 came from Caphtor, usually identified with Crete. The words ‘to this day’ in verse 22 suggest that some of these notes were written from a later time than Moses' speech.

The notes also carry a message for a frightened people. At Kadesh, Israel had refused the land because the people there were ‘as tall as the Anakites’. Here Moses points out that Edom, Moab and Ammon had each faced peoples like that and now lived in their lands. What Israel thought impossible, its neighbors had already seen happen.

Verse 14 marks the saddest boundary in the chapter. The Brook of Zered was the border between Edom and Moab. Israel crossed it only when the last of the men who refused the land had died. Thirty-eight years are passed over in two verses. The oath of chapter 1 has been kept.
passages.later:
Genesis traces both peoples to the daughters of Lot: “The older daughter gave birth to a son and named him Moab” (Genesis 19:37).

Ruth, the great-grandmother of King David, was a woman of Moab, and the book that bears her name tells how she came to trust Israel's God.

The prophet Amos told Israel that the LORD had moved other peoples as he moved them: “Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Arameans from Kir?” (Amos 9:7).
passages.asks: God guarded the land of peoples who did not worship him. Ask how you think about the people beside you who do not share your faith, and whether you believe God cares what happens to them. And think of the thirty-eight years. Ask what it means that God kept his people through a whole generation of waiting.

passages.t: Sihon: an offer of peace, and a war
passages.happening:
At the Arnon Valley the orders change. “See, I have delivered into your hand Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon, and his land. Begin to take possession of it and engage him in battle” (verse 24).

Moses first sends messengers ‘with an offer of peace’ (verse 26). The request is the one made to Edom and Moab: “Let us pass through your land; we will stay on the main road” (verse 27). Israel will pay for food and water.

“But Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass through, for the LORD your God had made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate” (verse 30). Sihon marches out with his whole army, and Israel defeats him at Jahaz (verses 32-33).

“At that time we captured all his cities and devoted to destruction the people of every city, including women and children. We left no survivors” (verse 34). Israel kept the livestock and the plunder. It did not go near the land of Ammon, ‘or any place that the LORD our God had forbidden’ (verse 37).
passages.hearers:
Sihon ruled land north of the Arnon, with his city at Heshbon. Numbers 21 tells the same battle more briefly.

The pattern of the chapter breaks here. Three peoples were to be left alone. This land God gives to Israel. Even so, Moses opens with words of peace. Later the law of war will require it: a city must be offered peace before it is attacked (20:10). Refusing passage on the main road was a hostile act, and Sihon went further and came out to fight.

Verse 30 says that God made Sihon's spirit stubborn. The same thing is said of Pharaoh in Exodus, where the text also says that Pharaoh hardened his own heart. The Bible holds the two together and does not explain how they fit.

Then comes verse 34. The words ‘devoted to destruction’ translate a Hebrew verb, charam. Something under this ban was given over wholly and could not be kept for ordinary use. Here it means that the people of the towns were killed. The verse says so itself: ‘including women and children’.

A new reader should not hurry past that sentence. The hard question below takes it up.

The last verse returns to restraint. Israel took what God gave and stopped at the borders God set. The chapter that tells of this war is the same chapter that three times forbids one.
passages.later:
Numbers tells the same refusal: “But Sihon would not let Israel pass through his territory. Instead, he gathered his whole army and went out to confront Israel in the wilderness” (Numbers 21:23).

Israel sang of this victory in its worship: ‘Sihon king of the Amorites’, with the answer, “His loving devotion endures forever” (Psalm 136:19).

The New Testament gives the church a different fight: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (Ephesians 6:12).
passages.hard:
How should a reader understand the killing of the people of Sihon's towns, ‘including women and children’, and the statement that God made Sihon stubborn?

This is one of the hardest verses in the book. It belongs with the wider question of the conquest, and Christians who receive these books as God's word read it in more than one way.

Some take the account as it stands. On this reading God, the judge of all the earth, judged a particular people at one point in history. God had told Abraham centuries before that his descendants would wait, ‘for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete’ (Genesis 15:16). Sihon was offered peace and chose war. This was never given as a general rule.

Others note that ancient reports of war, such as the Moabite king Mesha's inscription, used sweeping language of total destruction as an ordinary way of describing a victory. On this reading the words may not be a count of every person killed.

Others read these passages as God meeting an ancient people within the limits of their world, to be read in the light of Christ. Those who reject this reading say that it weakens the authority of Scripture.

Each reading has a cost, and these notes take no side. On any of them, the children remain the hardest part, and no answer makes that grief go away.

On the hardening of Sihon: many readers note that God gives people over to what they have already chosen, as with Pharaoh. Others stress God's purpose and do not deny that Sihon was responsible for what he did. The text says both things and leaves them side by side.

Several things can be said on every reading. The chapter itself forbids Israel to touch three other peoples. The war began when Sihon marched out. The Bible does not offer it as a pattern for later believers, and the New Testament tells God's people that their fight is not against flesh and blood.

No one may use these verses as a reason for violence against any person or people. They name a kingdom that passed away long ago, and they say nothing about any nation or conflict today.

A reader who finds this verse troubling is in good company. The site's pages on the violence of the Old Testament and on the command to destroy the Canaanites go further.
passages.asks: Israel was told plainly where it must stop: three peoples left in peace, and borders it was forbidden to cross. Ask where God has set limits on what you may take, and whether you keep them when you have the strength not to. And ask what you do with a verse like verse 34. It is better to say honestly what troubles you than to pretend it does not.
